| **797** | engine: re-pin content CIDs on sub-EOL renewal by threading `content_cids` into held records | Same `content_cids` plumbing (`facade.rs:1162`); likely subsumed or adjacent |
| **641** | web: land the Service Worker byte pipe and app-shell precache | Consumes `leaf_range_for_byte_range` (`read.rs:282`), currently uncalled |
| **794** | core: encode-side recursion depth bound is `debug_assert`-only | Same rule-8 class; named precedent in #812 |
| **786** | engine: wire `undo_dest_add_versioned` into the seq-CAS publish envelope | Needs the publish driver this slice would build — **collision** |
| **793** | engine: write-body structure sig epoch mismatch over-rejects read-rotated records | Gate-side, adjacent |
| **752** | engine: assemble the facade cold-start identity derivation and live-session wiring | #797 is "Part of #752"; parent for facade wiring |
| **635** | engine: implement rotation primitives, sweep, name wave, and grants | Owns `ScopeRootPublisher`/`WriteWavePublisher` (`rotation/rotate_write.rs:139-180`) — the *other* abstract publish port. **Risk of two publish drivers** |
| **665** | desktop: harden `StagingStore` unlink-ordering durability on Windows | Staged content bytes durability |
| **800** | engine: skip redundant owner-write-seed recovery on steady-state Current polls | Resolve-tick loop, same file |
| **655** | v2 build tracker | Umbrella (`Part of #655`) |

Also noted by recon, **not filed**: (a) the engine's mailbox routes `POST /mailbox`, `GET /mailbox`, `DELETE /mailbox/{id}` (`client.rs:327,338,359`) do not match the API's `/mailbox/messages` (`apps/api/src/mailbox/mailbox.controller.ts:30,58`, `openapi.json:294,383`) — will 404, no contract test covers it; (b) `crates/engine/src/api/mod.rs:6-11` and `api/types.rs:158-165` still claim the registry/content surface is "not yet implemented server-side (#624)" — stale; (c) quota gate uses `sumHostedBytes` while `GET /account/quota` reports `sumPinnedBytes` (`content.service.ts:265` vs `registry.service.ts:291`), so a client's local pre-flight prediction can disagree with the 413.

---

## 5. Open questions — the genuine forks

### Q1. Is this one slice or several? Where does the seam cut?

**Why it's a fork:** items 3–7 in §2 (queue drain, record authoring, block upload, child publish, child-ref authoring) are *not content-specific* — they are the entire missing write plane, needed equally by `mkdir`. Today `Create{content: None}` "succeeds" and publishes nothing. Framing this as "the content write slice" mis-scopes it.

Candidates: **(a)** one big slice; **(b)** split into `write-plane publish driver (metadata)` → `content sealing + upload` → `#812 guards`, where (b1) makes `mkdir` actually publish and is independently testable; **(c)** carve out a "publish a single child record" primitive first and drive both from it.

Recommendation to put to the human: **(b)**, because the metadata publish driver is provable end-to-end against #811's read path with zero content bytes, and #812's four guards attach cleanly to the record-authoring layer once it exists.

### Q2. Does the content path go through the op queue, or bypass it?

**Why it's a fork:** the blueprint is unambiguous that it goes through (`engine.md:208-211`, `CONTEXT.md:52`, `web-client.md:191-193` "one journaled op regardless of online state"), and the op model already carries `content_staging_key`. But the *sealed bytes* must be uploaded before publish, and upload requires the network. So the fork is really **when**: does the drain driver upload at drain time (offline-correct, but the content key is minted at command time and must survive in the op/staging plane), or does `Engine::command` seal-and-upload eagerly and only journal a CID?

Candidates: (a) seal at command time → stage sealed bytes → upload at drain (blueprint-aligned, requires the content key to persist across the boundary); (b) seal+upload at command time (breaks offline parity); (c) seal at command time, upload at command time when online, at drain when offline (two code paths, worst of both).

**Sub-fork with a security edge:** where does the per-version content key live between `Engine::command` and publish? It cannot be re-derived (KDF non-edge, `kdf/mod.rs:18-20`). Either it rides the `Op` (a plaintext secret in the durable op queue — the `Op` codec is serde_json, `op.rs:178-187`), or it goes into the `StagingStore` alongside the bytes, or it is held in memory (lost on crash → orphaned staged bytes, unrecoverable version). `staging.rs:40-42` currently guarantees "no plaintext user content ever lands in the staging store at rest" — a bare content key at rest is arguably worse.

### Q3. Chunk framing: engine or client?

**Why it's a fork:** `core.md:266-268` says core "ships the content-seal primitive over caller-framed chunks" and hands framing to the engine; `engine.md:483-487` confirms the engine frames. But #807/`web-client.md:189` says the UI hands a **`File` handle** (transferred), and the `Http` seam takes only `Option<Vec<u8>>` (`seams/http.rs:75-82`) with no streaming. So the whole file must materialize in the WASM worker's heap, be sealed, and then be copied again per upload.

Candidates: (a) engine frames from a full in-memory `Vec<u8>` (simplest, blows up on large files in a browser tab); (b) the client slices the `File` and feeds the engine chunk-at-a-time through a facade streaming API (contradicts "one journaled op", needs a new facade shape); (c) engine frames but the `Http` seam gains a streaming/`ReadableStream` body (a seam change; #641 is already parked on the wasm buffering issue, `seams/http.rs:143-148`).

This decision also fixes the answer to "what is the max uploadable file in v2.0" — currently bounded by RAM, and the API caps at 100 MiB (`app-setup.ts:8`).

### Q4. Upload before or after the op commits — and what is the rollback?

**Why it's a fork:** blocks must be uploaded and pinned before the record is published, or the read path gets a valid record pointing at unfetchable CIDs. But `register-first` (`CONTEXT.md:71`) says the name/CID batch registers *before* first publish. Meanwhile the API's `POST /content/upload` **already** creates the `pinned_cids` row (`content.service.ts:176-281`), and `POST /registry/register` also creates rows at `size: '0'` (`registry.service.ts:174-178`). So there are two ingress paths for a pin row and the ordering between them is not specified anywhere.

Candidates: (a) `upload(leaves) → upload(root) → upload(envelope) → register(name, contentCids) → publish`; (b) `register(name, contentCids) → upload → publish` (true register-first, but you must know the CIDs before uploading, which you do — `compute_cid` is local); (c) upload-only and let upload's own pin row satisfy inventory (skips name registration — violates register-first).

Rollback fork: if publish fails after upload, the uploaded blocks are pinned and quota-charged with no record referencing them. Is that GC'd via `retire`, left for the "registered-never-published orphan, alert-GC'd" residual (`CONTEXT.md:71`), or retried from the still-queued op?

### Q5. Which `PinMode`, and is the pre-flight quota check in or out?

**Why it's a fork:** `engine.md:474-476` says "the engine decides where bytes go" across Hosted/External/Dual, and `PinMode` is already defined (`content/provider.rs:25-32`) with zero consumers. `engine.md:469-470` explicitly marks the pre-flight quota query as **"judgment"** — i.e. an unmade decision. **Issue #705 is a landmine**: the moment `PinMode::Dual` is wired, `pre_flight_quota_check` (`retention.rs:32-45`) short-circuits on an account-level `advisory` boolean and would let hosted bytes skip the fail-fast check.

Candidates: (a) v2.0 ships Hosted only, `PinMode` stays dormant, #705 stays deferred; (b) ship Hosted + External, no Dual; (c) ship all three and fix #705 in-slice (advisory must track the byte path, not the account). Also: pre-flight quota call in (extra round trip, better UX, must handle the `sumHostedBytes`/`sumPinnedBytes` divergence) or out (rely on the authoritative 413)?

### Q6. Are chunk size and DAG shape frozen by this slice?

**Why it's a fork:** `engine.md:510-511` and `testing.md:296` say chunk size / DAG shape / retention defaults "freeze alongside the KAT manifest", and `profile.rs:36-38` calls `PRODUCTION = 1 MiB` an explicit placeholder. The DAG is currently flat/single-level (`dag.rs:12-16` names fan-out an open edge), which caps a file at ~108 GiB at 1 MiB chunks under the 4 MiB root cap (`limits.rs:12-14`). **Once a file is published with a given root shape, changing the shape is a wire-format break for already-published content.**

Candidates: (a) freeze 1 MiB + flat DAG now and add an engine-side KAT vector as part of this slice; (b) publish behind a versioned root (`chunkSize` is already in the manifest, so readers tolerate a change — but a fan-out level is *not* forward-compatible with the current `decode_root`); (c) defer the freeze and accept that pre-freeze published content may need migration.

### Q7. Does the read path re-fetch the just-written content, or does the write path seed the cache?

**Why it's a fork:** `read_content` (`facade.rs:1404-1519`) reads from the **base snapshot only** and returns `ContentUnavailable("content not yet published")` for a node with a pending op (`:1413-1427`). Right after an upload, the user immediately previews the file. Either the write path seeds `SnapshotCache`/base snapshot on publish success, or the UI eats a full resolve + gateway round trip for bytes it just held in memory.

Candidates: (a) publish success repaints the base snapshot (mirrors `project_child_version`, `sync/project.rs:50-63`) and the read goes over the network; (b) additionally cache the plaintext or sealed blocks locally; (c) do nothing and accept the latency. Note (b) reintroduces plaintext at rest, which `staging.rs:40-42` deliberately forbids.

### Q8. Cancel semantics.

**Why it's a fork:** `web-client.md:193-194` and #807 both require cancel "killing the op before publish", but no `Command` variant exists and the op queue has no cancel path (`remove_op` is only called from the undecodable sweep, `facade.rs:1024`). Candidates: (a) a new `Command::CancelOp { op_id }` — but `OpId` is a staging-store detail not exposed through the facade today; (b) cancel keyed on `NodeId`; (c) defer cancel to a follow-up and let #807 ship without it (contradicts its stated test "cancel kills the op").

### Q9. Which layer owns the #812 guards?

**Why it's a fork:** guard 3 ("`Version::new` and DAG `assemble` take `size` independently; seal/publish must tie them") can be enforced in **core** (make `Version::new` take a `SealedContent`-derived size, a core API change with KAT implications) or in the **engine** (a release-active check in `seal_content`/the publish path). Guards 1 and 4 similarly sit at either the core seal API or the engine's authoring layer. Choosing core means touching frozen encodings and the KAT manifest; choosing engine means the guarantee is per-callsite rather than structural.

### Q10. Does the drain driver share a publish port with rotation (#635)?

**Why it's a fork:** `rotation/rotate_write.rs:157-180` already defines `WriteWavePublisher` (register / is_republished / republish / retire / publish_repoint) and `grants/create.rs:51` references a `ScopeRootPublisher` — both abstract, both faked in tests, both awaiting "real wiring is #745/#746". If the content slice builds a *second*, concrete publish path over `net::publish::publish`, the codebase ends up with two publish drivers and two register-first implementations. Candidates: (a) build the concrete driver and later back the rotation traits with it; (b) implement the rotation traits first and route content publish through them; (c) let them diverge and reconcile later (a documented debt).

input.content:
## Destination

A settled design and a dependency-linked chain of build slices covering the engine's **write plane** end to end: from a user mutation entering `Engine::command` to a record published, registered, and readable by the resolve/read path landed in #811. Content bytes are one layer of that plane, not the whole of it.

The map is done when nothing is left to decide — the slices can be filed against #655 and built.

## Notes

**Domain:** `crates/engine` (write plane, content plane, sync/op-queue, net/publish), `crates/core` (content-seal primitive, envelope/read-body encode), the engine's hand-written API client, and the API's upload/registry/quota surface.

**Skills every session should consult:** `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` by default; `/research` for the AFK research tickets; `/codebase-design` and `/design-an-interface` for the shared publish port.

**Standing preferences for this effort:**

- `CONTEXT.md` is the ubiquitous language — use its terms exactly (op queue, pending-op overlay, dead-letter, register-first, name inventory, advisory pin row, content key, adoption gate, floor law, eager set).
- `blueprint/core.md` and `blueprint/engine.md` are normative; where they name an "open edge" or "judgment", that is an unmade decision this map owns.
- AGENTS.md rule 8 (encode/decode fail-closed symmetry, release-active `Err`, never `debug_assert!`) and rule 7 (zeroize at the terminal owner only) bind every decision here.
- Determinism is injected — entropy, time, and policy enter as seam traits; never a direct clock or RNG.
- This is a **planning** map. It produces decisions and a slice chain, not the implementation.

**Scoping calls already made (2026-07-27):**

- Chunk size, DAG fan-out shape, and retention defaults are **in scope** — this effort freezes them, with an engine-side KAT vector for the DAG root block.
- The pin-provider layer ships **all three** `PinMode`s (Hosted, External, Dual), with the #705 advisory-quota fix folded in.
- The publish driver is **one shared port**, later backing rotation's `WriteWavePublisher` / `ScopeRootPublisher` (#635) — not a second register-first implementation.

## Why this map exists

Reconnaissance (2026-07-27) established that the gap is not content-specific. The engine has **no production write plane at all**:

- `sync::rebase::replay` (`crates/engine/src/sync/rebase.rs:138`) has no `src/` caller.
- `sync/tick.rs::run_tick_loop` (`crates/engine/src/sync/tick.rs:178`) has no `src/` caller.
- `seal_read_body` / `encode_envelope` appear in the engine only inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules.
- `ApiClient::upload` and `ApiClient::quota` (`crates/engine/src/api/client.rs:292`, `:283`) have zero production callers.
- The content plane's write half — `seal_content` (`content/mod.rs:86`), `frame_and_seal` (`content/chunk.rs:78`), `dag::assemble` (`content/dag.rs:106`) — is built and KAT-frozen in core, and entirely orphaned.

Consequence: today a plain `mkdir` stages an op, emits `SnapshotUpdated`, and publishes nothing — the op sits in the queue forever. `Create { content: None }` is not implemented either; it fails silently rather than returning `Unimplemented`.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

_None yet._

## Not yet specified

- **Optimistic overlay projection for content** — a pending upload renders with no size and no mtime (`sync/overlay.rs:48-52` bumps `content_version` only). What the UI shows between command and publish depends on where the upload boundary lands.
- **Upload-side op progress and `OpId` exposure** — `OpPhase` has only `Download*` variants (`facade.rs:438-445`) and `emit_op_progress` hardcodes `op_id: None` (`facade.rs:1524`). #807 needs per-file progress keyed on the upload's op id; the shape follows the drain driver.
- **Dead-letter population from replay** — `dead_letters` is filled only from the cold-start undecodable sweep (`facade.rs:1016`); `ReplayReport::dead_letters` never reaches it. Becomes specifiable once the drain driver exists.
- **Version retention and prune** — the blueprint's "keep all versions within quota, with an explicit user-initiated prune op" needs a concrete op and policy. `content/retention.rs` has `plan_prune` with no caller.

## Question

Where does the upload boundary sit relative to the durable op journal — does `Engine::command` seal and stage, with upload deferred to the drain driver, or does it seal and upload eagerly and journal only the resulting CIDs?

This is the load-bearing decision of the map: the drain driver's shape, content key custody, cancel semantics, and the pending-overlay projection all follow from it.

## What is fixed already

`blueprint/engine.md:208-211` and `web-client.md:189-193` are unambiguous that a content write is **one journaled op regardless of online state**, and the op model already carries the seam: `OpKind::Create { content_staging_key: Option<Vec<u8>> }` and `OpKind::UpdateContent { content_staging_key: Vec<u8> }` (`crates/engine/src/sync/op.rs:37-82`). No bytes and no CIDs ride an op by design (`op.rs:11-13`). `stage_op(store, profile, op, upload: Option<&[u8]>)` (`sync/staging.rs:47-83`) already writes staged bytes **before** enqueuing the op, and `staging.rs:40-42` guarantees no plaintext user content lands in the staging store at rest.

So the fork is not *whether* it goes through the queue — it is *when the bytes leave the device*.

## Candidates

1. **Seal at command time, upload at drain.** Blueprint-aligned, offline-correct. Requires the per-version content key to survive the durable boundary (see the blocked custody ticket) and requires the drain driver to own the upload retry.
2. **Seal and upload at command time, journal the CIDs.** Simpler key handling — the key never outlives the call. Breaks offline parity: a queued op could never be created offline.
3. **Hybrid — upload at command time when online, at drain when offline.** Two code paths for the same op; likely the worst of both, but should be considered and rejected explicitly rather than by omission.

## Notes for the resolving session

`stage_and_notify` (`facade.rs:1581-1597`) currently hardcodes `upload = None` and maps `StageOutcome::RejectedOverBudget` onto an internal `EngineError::Seam`. There is no `EngineError::OverBudget` variant (`facade.rs:449-512`), so the blueprint's law that "only new uploads fail fast past the budget; metadata ops queue unbounded" (`engine.md:233-235`) is currently unexpressible — whichever candidate wins, that error surface needs designing here.

## Question

How do the API's two pin-row ingress paths interact, and which byte total is authoritative for quota?

`POST /content/upload` creates a `pinned_cids` row as part of its own transaction (`apps/api/src/content/content.service.ts:176-281`), and `POST /registry/register` also creates rows, at `size: '0'` (`apps/api/src/registry/registry.service.ts:174-178`). The ordering and interaction between the two is not specified anywhere. Register-first (`CONTEXT.md:71`) says the name and CID batch registers before first publish — but by then upload may already have made the row.

## What to establish

1. What happens today, concretely, for each ordering: upload-then-register, register-then-upload, and register-only for a CID that is never uploaded. Does the second write update, conflict, no-op, or duplicate? What does the `size` column end up as?
2. The quota surfaces disagree: the upload gate sums via `sumHostedBytes` (`content.service.ts:265`) while `GET /account/quota` reports `sumPinnedBytes` (`registry.service.ts:291`). Establish whether a client's local pre-flight prediction can legitimately disagree with the authoritative 413, and by how much.
3. What the advisory flag means for BYO (`advisory: true` per `blueprint/engine.md:464-470`) and which of the two totals it tracks — this is the crux of #705.
4. Whether the "registered-never-published orphan, alert-GC'd" residual (`CONTEXT.md:71`) already covers the rollback case where blocks are uploaded and pinned but publish then fails.

## Method

Read the API source and its tests; run the real endpoints against a local stack if that is faster than reading (see the repo's local e2e recipes). Do not change any code. Capture findings as a research note and link it here.

## Why it is a decision blocker

The register/upload/publish ordering ticket and the pin-provider ticket both hang on these facts. Neither can be decided from the blueprint alone, because the blueprint describes register-first as an ordering law without saying what the upload endpoint's own pin row does to it.

## Question

What is the memory model for a content write — and therefore, what is the largest file v2.0 can upload?

## Why it is a fork

`blueprint/core.md:266-268` gives core the content-seal primitive "over caller-framed chunks" and hands framing to the engine; `engine.md:483-487` confirms the engine frames. But `web-client.md:189` has the UI hand over a **`File` handle** (transferred, never copied through React state), and the `Http` seam takes only `Option<Vec<u8>>` with no streaming (`crates/engine/src/seams/http.rs:75-82`, `:131`, `:152`).

So today the whole file must materialise in the WASM worker's heap, be framed and sealed into a second full copy, then be copied again per upload — `ApiClient::upload` does `content.to_vec()` (`api/client.rs:298`) and `request_authed` clones once more for the 401 retry (`client.rs:438`). That is up to 3x resident for a route the API caps at 100 MiB (`apps/api/src/app-setup.ts:8`).

## Candidates

1. **Engine frames from a full in-memory `Vec<u8>`.** Simplest, matches the current seam set, and puts a hard RAM ceiling on file size in a browser tab. Requires stating that ceiling as a product constraint.
2. **The client slices the `File` and feeds the engine chunk-at-a-time** through a new facade shape. Bounded memory, but sits awkwardly against "one journaled op regardless of online state" and needs a new command surface.
3. **Engine frames, but the `Http` seam gains a streaming body.** A seam change affecting every implementation (browser, desktop, fakes). Note #641 is already parked on a related wasm buffering problem (`seams/http.rs:143-148`).

## What resolving looks like

Pick the model, state the resulting maximum file size explicitly, and say whether the per-upload copies (`client.rs:298`, `:438`) are acceptable or must be eliminated. If a seam change is chosen, name what it does to the desktop and fake implementations.

## Question

What should the chunk size and DAG fan-out shape be, and what retention defaults go with them?

This is the research half of the freeze; the decision itself is a separate blocked ticket.

## Constraints to work within

- `ContentProfile::PRODUCTION` is 1 MiB and `profile.rs:36-38` explicitly calls it a placeholder. `CI` is 16 bytes.
- The DAG is currently flat and single-level — `dag.rs:12-16` names fan-out an open edge. Root shape is det-CBOR `{ chunkSize, size, links[] }` with codec `0x71` (`content/dag.rs:79-81`, `:120-124`).
- `MAX_RESOLVED_RECORD_BYTES` is 4 MiB (`content/limits.rs:17`), which with 1 MiB flat chunks caps a single file at roughly 108 GiB.
- The API caps an upload at 100 MiB (`apps/api/src/app-setup.ts:8`).
- `blueprint/engine.md:483-487` requires the DAG be "shaped so ranged block/CAR fetches map chunk-aligned" — `leaf_range_for_byte_range` (`content/read.rs:282-305`) already assumes that and is the future consumer via #641.
- `engine.md:510-511` and `testing.md:296` say these values freeze alongside the KAT manifest.

## What to establish

1. What chunk sizes comparable content-addressed systems use and why (IPFS/UnixFS defaults, Blake3 chunking, common CDN range-request granularity), and what the tradeoff curve looks like between per-chunk overhead, ranged-fetch waste, and root-block size.
2. Whether a flat DAG is defensible for v2.0 given the 4 MiB root cap, or whether a fan-out level is needed — and critically, whether adding one later is forward-compatible with today's `decode_root` (`dag.rs:159-199`). Initial reading says it is **not**, which would make this a genuine wire-format commitment.
3. What retention defaults are workable against "keep all versions within quota, with an explicit user-initiated prune op" (`engine.md:483-490`) — `content/retention.rs` has `plan_prune` and `pre_flight_quota_check` with no callers.
4. What an engine-side KAT vector for an assembled DAG root block would need to pin. None exists today; `crates/engine/tests/` has no content-plane test file, only inline round-trips at `dag.rs:263-407`.

Capture findings as a research note and link it here.

## Question

After a successful publish, does the write path seed the base snapshot and cache, or does the user eat a full resolve plus gateway round trip for bytes the device just held?

## Why it is a fork

`read_content` reads from the **base snapshot only** and returns `ContentUnavailable("content not yet published")` for any node with a pending op targeting it (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:1413-1427`). The realistic sequence is: user uploads a file, then immediately previews it. Unless publish success repaints the base snapshot, that preview either fails or takes a full `resolve` plus per-leaf gateway fetch for content that was in memory moments earlier.

## Candidates

1. **Publish success repaints the base snapshot**, mirroring what `project_child_version` already does for a read (`facade.rs:1386-1388`, `sync/project.rs:50-63`). The read then goes over the network but at least resolves.
2. **Additionally cache locally** — plaintext or sealed blocks. Note this reintroduces content at rest, which `sync/staging.rs:40-42` deliberately forbids for the staging store; if the answer is "cache sealed blocks", say where and under what budget.
3. **Do nothing** and accept the latency, on the grounds that the resolve is correct and the cost is a one-time round trip.

## What resolving looks like

Pick a candidate and state the invariant it establishes about what a client may believe about its own just-published write without re-resolving. Note that the adoption gate (AGENTS.md rule 6) applies to every resolved record — any local seeding must not become a way to skip it.

## Question

Where does the per-version content key live between `Engine::command` and publish, and what is the crash-recovery story for a staged-but-unpublished version?

## Why it is a fork with a security edge

A content key is a stated **KDF non-edge** — random per version, never derived (`crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:18-20`, `core.md:197-198`, `CONTEXT.md:10`). It is minted from raw entropy at `content/chunk.rs:31-35` and is `ZeroizeOnDrop`. So it **cannot be recovered** — if it is lost between sealing and publishing, the staged bytes are permanently unopenable garbage.

If the upload boundary lands after the durable journal, something must carry that key across the boundary. Every option has a cost:

1. **It rides the `Op`.** The op codec is serde_json (`sync/op.rs:178-187`), so this puts a bare symmetric content key in plaintext in the durable op queue. Arguably worse than the plaintext content that `sync/staging.rs:40-42` explicitly forbids at rest.
2. **It goes into the `StagingStore` alongside the sealed bytes.** Same at-rest exposure, different drawer — but at least colocated with what it opens, and covered by the staging budget and GC.
3. **It is held in memory only.** No at-rest exposure; a crash between command and publish orphans the staged bytes with no way to recover the version. Needs a GC story (`orphan_staging_keys`, `staging.rs:88-111`) and an answer for what the user sees.
4. **Seal late** — journal the plaintext-free intent, mint the key at drain. Changes what "staged bytes" means and may collapse into the eager-upload candidate.

## What resolving looks like

Pick where the key lives, state the at-rest exposure that choice accepts, and define the crash-recovery behaviour: what happens to staged bytes whose key is gone, who GCs them, and what the user is told. Confirm the terminal-owner zeroization rule (AGENTS.md rule 7) still holds across whatever boundary is chosen.

## Question

What is the exact ordering of upload, register, and publish — and what is the rollback when a step fails partway?

## Why it is a fork

Blocks must be uploaded and pinned before a record is published, or the read path resolves a valid record pointing at unfetchable CIDs. But **register-first** (`CONTEXT.md:71`, `blueprint/engine.md:464-470` — "register-first ordering is built into the publish pipeline, not left to callers") says the name and CID batch registers before first publish. Meanwhile the upload endpoint creates its own pin row. The CIDs are known locally before any bytes move, because `compute_cid` is a local computation (`crates/core/src/content/cid.rs:70`) — so more orderings are available than are obviously correct.

## Candidates

1. `upload(leaves) -> upload(root) -> upload(envelope) -> register(name, contentCids) -> publish`
2. `register(name, contentCids) -> upload -> publish` — true register-first, viable because CIDs are computable before upload
3. Upload-only, letting the upload endpoint's own pin row satisfy inventory — skips name registration and violates register-first, but should be rejected explicitly

## The rollback half

If publish fails after upload, blocks are pinned and quota-charged with nothing referencing them. Decide which applies:

- GC via `retire` (`net/retire.rs:24`, live today)
- the "registered-never-published orphan, alert-GC'd" residual (`CONTEXT.md:71`)
- retry from the still-queued op, since the op has not been removed

Also decide the symmetric case: register succeeded, upload failed. And what the op queue does in each — retry, dead-letter with bytes preserved (`engine.md:231-235`), or drop.

## Existing machinery

`net::publish::publish` (`net/publish.rs:115`) already implements register-first, floor-plus-one CAS, fanout PUT, and confirm-by-re-resolve — but is only ever called by liveness (`net/liveness.rs:28`) and revival (`net/revival.rs:15`). `PublishRequest.content_cids` (`net/publish.rs:38-53`) exists and every production producer passes an empty vec (`facade.rs:1162` — that is #797).

A new child also needs first-publish-at-sequence-1 semantics (`core.md:207`) plus the parent folder record republished with the new child ref.

## Question

Freeze the content format: what are the committed chunk size, DAG fan-out shape, and retention defaults, and what does the engine-side KAT vector pin?

The scoping call on 2026-07-27 put this freeze **in scope** for this effort. This ticket makes the call; its research blocker gathers the numbers.

## What must come out of this

1. **Chunk size** — a committed value replacing the `PRODUCTION = 1 MiB` placeholder (`content/profile.rs:36-38`), with the reasoning recorded.
2. **DAG shape** — flat single-level, or a fan-out level. `dag.rs:12-16` names this an open edge. If the research confirms a fan-out level is not forward-compatible with today's `decode_root` (`dag.rs:159-199`), then shipping flat is a wire-format commitment that must be made knowingly, with the resulting maximum file size stated.
3. **Retention defaults** — concrete policy for "keep all versions within quota, with an explicit user-initiated prune op" (`engine.md:483-490`), and whether the prune op is part of this map's slice chain or a later effort.
4. **The KAT vector** — what an engine-side frozen vector for an assembled DAG root block asserts. None exists today; `crates/engine/tests/` has no content-plane test file. `testing.md:296` and `engine.md:510-511` both say these freeze alongside the KAT manifest.

## Constraint to respect

The shape must keep ranged block and CAR fetches chunk-aligned (`engine.md:483-487`), because `leaf_range_for_byte_range` (`content/read.rs:282-305`) already assumes it and #641 is the downstream consumer. The freeze must not foreclose streaming media even though streaming itself is out of scope for this map.

## Question

What is the shape of the one shared publish port — the driver that authors and publishes a record, serving both the content write plane and rotation's existing abstract ports?

The scoping call on 2026-07-27 chose **one shared port** over building a second concrete driver: the codebase must not end up with two register-first implementations.

## What it has to serve

- **The write plane's drain path**: take applied ops from `replay` and, per op, author a read-body, seal it, encode and sign the envelope, derive the child's own `ipnsName`, upload the head block, register, and publish. None of this exists in production today — `seal_read_body` and `encode_envelope` appear in `crates/engine/src` only inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules.
- **Rotation's ports** (#635): `WriteWavePublisher` (register / `is_republished` / republish / retire / `publish_repoint`) at `rotation/rotate_write.rs:157-180`, and `ScopeRootPublisher` referenced at `grants/create.rs:51`. Both abstract, both faked in tests, both awaiting real wiring.
- **Liveness and revival**, which already call `net::publish::publish` directly (`net/liveness.rs:28`, `net/revival.rs:15`).

## The design questions

1. Does the shared port sit **above** `net::publish::publish` (a record-authoring layer that delegates the CAS/register/PUT mechanics) or **replace** it?
2. Is the unit "publish one record" or "publish a batch"? Rotation's name wave is inherently batched; a single content write is not.
3. Where does child `ipnsName` derivation live — `SessionIdentity::write_name_signer` (`session.rs:147-152`) is currently used only for the root, by liveness and resolve.
4. What does the port need for first-publish-at-sequence-1 (`core.md:207`) versus CAS-at-expected-sequence, and does the caller or the port decide which?
5. How do #786 (`undo_dest_add_versioned` into the seq-CAS publish envelope) and #797 (`content_cids` into held records) land — subsumed by this port, or separate slices against it?

## Method

Use `/codebase-design` and `/design-an-interface`. The output is an interface, its seam boundary, and a statement of which existing call sites collapse into it.

## Question

How does the pin-provider layer work across all three `PinMode`s, and what is the fix that makes advisory quota track the byte path rather than the account?

The scoping call on 2026-07-27 put **all three modes** (Hosted, External, Dual) in scope, with #705 folded into this effort rather than deferred.

## Current state

`PinMode { Hosted, External, Dual }`, `ByoIpfsConfig`, `test_connection`, and `validate_endpoint` all exist at `crates/engine/src/content/provider.rs:25-160` with **zero consumers anywhere**. `pre_flight_quota_check` and `plan_prune` (`content/retention.rs:32-84`) have no callers. `ApiClient::quota` (`api/client.rs:283`) has no production caller. There is no `PinProvider` seam trait — `provider.rs` is config plus a prober, not a seam.

`blueprint/engine.md:474-479`: "the engine decides where bytes go; **every mode's publish flow still traverses registration**. `ByoIpfsConfig` stays sealed in vault settings."

## The #705 landmine

`pre_flight_quota_check` short-circuits on an account-level `advisory` boolean. The moment `PinMode::Dual` is wired, the hosted leg of a dual write would skip the fail-fast check, because the account reads as advisory while real hosted bytes are moving. The fix must make advisory track the **byte path**, not the account.

## Decisions to make

1. Does the pin-provider layer become a **seam trait**, or a concrete dispatch over `Http`? Note BYO endpoints are arbitrary third-party hosts (Kubo/PSA/Pinata), which has trust-boundary and DoS implications the security review will probe.
2. Where does `ByoIpfsConfig` live at rest, given it "stays sealed in vault settings"?
3. What does Dual mean on partial failure — hosted succeeds and external fails, or the reverse? Is one leg authoritative for publish to proceed?
4. Is the pre-flight quota query **in or out**? `engine.md:469-470` explicitly marks it "judgment" — an unmade decision. It costs a round trip and buys fail-fast UX, but must handle the `sumHostedBytes` / `sumPinnedBytes` divergence its research blocker establishes.
5. What `retire` and prune mean for externally-pinned bytes the API never held.

## Question

Which layer owns #812's four encode-side fail-closed guards — `crates/core`'s seal API, or the engine's record-authoring layer?

## Why it is a fork

AGENTS.md rule 8 requires every decode-side hard reject to have a matching **release-active** `Err` on the produce path — never `debug_assert!`. #812 lists four such debts, each explicitly waiting on the write plane:

1. **Grant section on a child envelope** — child adoption rejects any envelope carrying a `grantSection` key (`has_grant_section`, `crates/core/src/seal/envelope.rs`); child envelope sealing must refuse to attach one.
2. **Kind transplant** — `read_content` rejects a sealed body kind disagreeing with the parent's `ChildRef.kind` (`facade.rs:1498-1504`); child-ref authoring must enforce the match.
3. **Version size versus manifest size** — `open_content` rejects `manifest.size != version.size` (`content/mod.rs:169-175`). Today `Version::new` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:156-169`) and `dag::assemble` take `size` independently; seal and publish must tie them.
4. **Child-ref `ipnsName` well-formedness** — the read path parses canonical base36 fail-closed (`facade.rs:1434-1441`); authoring must emit exactly that form.

Guard 3 is the clearest illustration of the fork. Enforcing it in **core** means changing `Version::new` to take something `SealedContent`-derived, which touches a frozen encoding and the KAT manifest — but makes the invariant structural and unbypassable. Enforcing it in the **engine** is a release-active check at the authoring call site — cheaper, but the guarantee is per-callsite and a future second caller can miss it. Guards 1 and 4 sit at the same choice.

## What resolving looks like

Decide per guard (they need not all land in the same layer), and say for each whether it is structural (the wrong state is unrepresentable) or checked (the wrong state returns `Err`). Every guard needs a test that fires in a **release** build — state how, following the `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` `assert_children_unique` convention.

Related precedent: #794 (core encode-side recursion depth bound is `debug_assert`-only, unbounded in release) is the same rule-8 class and is still open.

## Question

What are cancel semantics for an in-flight write, and what identity does the facade expose to address one?

## Why it is a fork

`blueprint/web-client.md:193-194` and #807 both require that "cancel is a facade command killing the op before publish", and #807 carries a test for it. But no `Command` variant exists (`facade.rs:235-350`), and the op queue has no cancel path — `remove_op` is called only from the cold-start undecodable sweep (`facade.rs:1024`).

There is also no addressable op identity at the facade boundary: `OpId` is a staging-store detail, and `emit_op_progress` hardcodes `op_id: None` (`facade.rs:1524`). Meanwhile #807 needs per-file upload progress keyed on the op id, so the identity question and the cancel question are the same question.

## Candidates

1. **`Command::CancelOp { op_id }`** — requires promoting `OpId` into the facade's public surface, which then also serves progress events.
2. **Cancel keyed on `NodeId`** — no new identity, but ambiguous when several ops target one node, and there is no obvious answer for which is cancelled.
3. **Defer cancel** and let #807 ship without it — contradicts its stated test and the blueprint, so it needs an explicit override if chosen.

## What resolving looks like

Decide the identity and the command, then define the semantics precisely: what cancel does to staged bytes (removed, or preserved like a dead-letter under `engine.md:231-235`), what it does to an op mid-upload versus mid-publish, whether it is best-effort or guaranteed before a point of no return, and what event the UI sees.

But no `Command` variant exists (`facade.rs:235-350`), and the op queue has no cancel path — `remove_op` is called only from the cold-start undecodable sweep (`facade.rs:1024`).

There is also no addressable op identity at the facade boundary: `OpId` is a staging-store detail, and `emit_op_progress` hardcodes `op_id: None` (`facade.rs:1524`). Meanwhile #807 needs per-file upload progress keyed on the op id, so the identity question and the cancel question are the same question.

## Candidates

1. **`Command::CancelOp { op_id }`** — requires promoting `OpId` into the facade's public surface, which then also serves progress events.
2. **Cancel keyed on `NodeId`** — no new identity, but ambiguous when several ops target one node, and there is no obvious answer for which is cancelled.
3. **Defer cancel** and let #807 ship without it — contradicts its stated test and the blueprint, so it needs an explicit override if chosen.

## What resolving looks like

Decide the identity and the command, then define the semantics precisely: what cancel does to staged bytes (removed, or preserved like a dead-letter under `engine.md:231-235`), what it does to an op mid-upload versus mid-publish, whether it is best-effort or guaranteed before a point of no return, and what event the UI sees.

input.content:
## Defect

All three of the engine API client's mailbox methods target routes the API does not serve. Every one will 404 on first use.

| Client method | Path sent | Path served |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mailbox_post` (`crates/engine/src/api/client.rs:306`, path at `:327`) | `POST /mailbox` | `POST /mailbox/messages` |
| `mailbox_poll` (`client.rs:336`, path at `:338`) | `GET /mailbox` | `GET /mailbox/messages` |
| `mailbox_ack` (`client.rs:357`, path at `:359`) | `DELETE /mailbox/{id}` | `DELETE /mailbox/messages/{id}` |

The API side is `@Controller('mailbox')` with `@Post('messages')`, `@Get('messages')`, and `@Delete('messages/:id')` (`apps/api/src/mailbox/mailbox.controller.ts:30,34,58,72`). `apps/api/openapi.json` declares only `/mailbox/messages` and `/mailbox/messages/{id}`.

## Why it was not caught

The contract suite has **no mailbox coverage at all** — `grep -rn mailbox crates/contract/tests/` returns nothing. Per AGENTS.md the live contract suite is the enforcement mechanism for the API contract, since there are no generated clients, so this is a gap in the gate rather than a flake.

The mismatch is latent today only because no production code calls these methods yet — the grants/mailbox engine logic that would exercise them has not been wired.

## Fix

1. Correct the three paths in `crates/engine/src/api/client.rs`.
2. Add mailbox coverage to the contract suite so the route set is enforced going forward — post, poll, and ack against a real API instance.

## Provenance

Found during reconnaissance for the write-plane wayfinder map #813, and recorded there as out of scope for that effort.

content.text:
Facts first — and they change the shape of this ticket.

The landed code has **already committed to candidate 1**, in contract text, not just by implication:

- `sync/staging.rs:40-42`: "`upload` is the **already-sealed** content payload (core's content-seal runs upstream in the content plane); no plaintext user content ever lands in the staging store at rest." Sealing happens *before* staging, i.e. at command time.
- `sync/op.rs:11-13`: "Content bytes never live in an op… the bytes sit in the staging store behind the profile budget."
- The staging budget exists specifically so an **offline** device can stage an upload — which only makes sense if upload is deferred.

So candidate 2 (seal and upload eagerly, journal CIDs) is already excluded by landed code plus `engine.md:208-211`, and candidate 3 collapses with it. There is no live three-way fork here.

But establishing that surfaced a sharper fork the ticket didn't anticipate, and it's a real one:

`put_staged_bytes(key, bytes)` stores **one opaque blob under one key** (`seams/staging_store.rs:38`), and `Op` carries exactly **one** `content_staging_key` (`op.rs:46`, `:81`). But `SealedContent` is *three* things — `{ content_cid, root_block, leaves: Vec<SealedChunk> }` (`content/mod.rs:48-56`), where `leaves` is N separately-CID'd blocks. So something has to reconcile "one key, one blob" with "N+1 blocks", and nothing in the landed code says what.

## 1. JSON shapes

**Manifest** — `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/crates/core/kat/manifest.json`, top level (manifest.json:1-4, 433): `manifestVersion` (int, pinned 1), `profile` (`"cipherbox/v2 det-cbor"`), then one section per plane: `codecs`, `structureTags`, `kdf`, `suite`, `seal`, `ipns`, `payload`, `grant`, `content`. A family entry is one of two shapes — accept (`FileCount`) or reject (`RejectSection`, adds `checks`). The whole content section (manifest.json:394-432):

```json
"content": {
  "cidCodec": 85, "cidMultihash": 30, "cidLen": 36,
  "seal":       { "file": "vectors/content/seal.json", "count": 3 },
  "sealReject": { "file": "vectors/content/seal_reject.json", "count": 3,
                  "checks": ["seal-open-failed", "truncated"] },
  "cid":        { "file": "vectors/content/cid.json", "count": 4 },
  "cidReject":  { "file": "vectors/content/cid_reject.json", "count": 5,
                  "checks": ["content-cid-mismatch"] }, ...
}
```

**Vector file** — always a top-level JSON *array* of flat objects, `name` first, `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` per struct (kat_manifest.rs:268-327). **All binary is lowercase hex** (`hex::encode`); the only non-hex encodings are CID strings (multibase base32, `cidStr`) and small integers left as JSON numbers (`codec`). Content CID vector (`vectors/content/cid.json:15-20`), the closest existing analogue to a DAG root:

```json
{ "name": "cid-dag-root-nonraw-codec",
  "codec": 113,
  "sealed": "617373656d626c6564206461672d726f6f74206e6f6465206279746573",
  "cid": "01711e20469f95275785ff4265858b4963283402fbcfb0c73b90d085f6ed61e4b741fdb7" }
```

Reject vectors add exactly two fields: `"check"` (the crate's `err.check()` string) and `"class"` (`"trust"` | `"malformed"`) — `vectors/content/seal_reject.json:1-9`.

## 2. Harness invariants (`/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/crates/core/tests/kat_manifest.rs`)

- **No filesystem** — manifest and every fixture are `include_str!`'d into a `FIXTURES` table (kat_manifest.rs:50-56). This is why the same suite runs on wasm.
- **wasm parity** — on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` the harness shadows `test` with `wasm_bindgen_test` (kat_manifest.rs:16-17), so all `#[test]`s run unchanged under wasm-bindgen-test-runner; wasm32-wasip1 uses libtest.
- **Missing/extra vector fails** — `fixture_table_matches_manifest_files` (kat_manifest.rs:1125-1189) builds the list of every `file` the manifest references and asserts set equality with `FIXTURES`, plus no file referenced twice. A new vector file must be added in *three* places: manifest section, `FIXTURES`, and the `referenced` array.
- **Counts are exact** — `vector_counts_are_exact` (1190) and per-family `assert_eq!(vectors.len(), m.<sect>.count)` + `assert!(!vectors.is_empty())` (e.g. 3754-3766).
- **Names unique per file** — 1210-1241 and a `BTreeSet` name check inside each family test.
- **Reject `checks` list == set of `check` values in the file**, asserted as `BTreeSet` equality (3797-3820), and `every_crate_check_is_pinned_by_a_vector_family` (1318-1384) requires every string in `TrustViolation::CHECKS ∪ Malformed::CHECKS` to be covered by some reject family — the only permitted exception is `unknown-field-collision`.
- **Determinism/freeze** — accept tests recompute from inputs and compare hex against the frozen field, e.g. `assert_eq!(hex::encode(&sealed), v.sealed)` (3775-3780) and `assert_eq!(hex::encode(&cid), v.cid)` (3862-3867); CID tests also assert `cid.len() == CONTENT_CID_LEN` and the 4-byte prefix `[0x01, v.codec, CONTENT_CID_MULTIHASH, 0x20]` (3869-3874), then `verify_cid` round-trips.
- **Manifest constants pinned to crate constants** — `content_cid_codec_bytes_are_frozen` (3734-3752) asserts `m.content.cidCodec == CONTENT_CID_CODEC == 0x55`, etc.
- Vectors regenerate only via the committed generator `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/crates/core/examples/kat_gen.rs` (content section at kat_gen.rs:215-290, 901-951) — a vector diff without a generator diff fails review by convention.

## 3. Naming / ID conventions

Directory = plane (`codec/ contact/ content/ grant/ hpke/ ipns/ kdf/ payload/ seal/`); file = `<family>.json` for accept and `<family>_reject.json` for fail-closed, with `_accept` explicit where a plane has several accept families (`read_body_accept.json`, `cid_str_accept.json`). Manifest key is the camelCase of the filename (`cidStrAccept` ↔ `cid_str_accept.json`). Vector `name` is kebab-case and describes the case, prefixed by family: `chunk-nonempty`, `chunk-256-bytes`, `cid-sealed-chunk`, `cid-dag-root-nonraw-codec`, `cid-str-empty-input`; reject names describe the tamper: `tampered-ciphertext`, `truncated-below-nonce-tag`. Full directory listing is the 9 dirs / 44 files enumerated above.

## 4. Engine hook: none

The KAT regime is **core-only**. `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/crates/engine/tests/` exists (adoption_gate.rs, conformance_fakes.rs, facade.rs, floor_atomic.rs, grants_mailbox.rs, net.rs, sync.rs) but has **no KAT harness, no manifest, no vectors dir**. The only engine mentions of "KAT" are prose: `crates/engine/src/content/dag.rs:10` ("one codec and one KAT set"), `crates/engine/src/content/profile.rs:3`, `crates/engine/tests/net.rs:43` and `adoption_gate.rs:45` ("KAT-style injected values" — inline fixture constants, not manifest-driven). The engine's discipline is the deterministic simulation harness (blueprint/testing.md:84-100), described as "hard-asserted the same way the KAT manifest is". The existing engine/core seam for a DAG root is already vector-shaped: `dag.rs:106-135` builds a canonical CBOR map with keys chunkSize/size/links and calls `compute_cid(DAG_ROOT_CODEC = 0x71, &root_block)` — and manifest.json already carries one non-raw-codec CID vector (`cid-dag-root-nonraw-codec`, codec 113 = 0x71) that pins core's side of exactly that call.

## 5. Blueprint on freezing

- blueprint/core.md:228-256 — the KAT regime: one machine-checked manifest enumerating every frozen encoding, accept+reject for every codec, separation KAT, fixed-parameter full-envelope KATs, anti-vacuity (counts + coverage hard-asserted, generators committed), "WASM is the residual parity surface".
- blueprint/core.md:266-271 (Open edges) — content chunking format is engine-owned; core ships only the content-seal primitive over caller-framed chunks. Context strings, struct-tag bytes, and fixtures "freeze in the KAT manifest at build time".
- blueprint/engine.md:509-511 — the load-bearing line for your question: "**Chunk size, DAG shape, retention defaults** — the judgment above needs numbers; freeze alongside the KAT manifest and testing strategy." So DAG shape/chunk size are explicitly listed as open edges whose eventual numbers get frozen into the KAT manifest.
- blueprint/testing.md:62-82 — CI wiring: `cargo test` runs the full KAT suite natively **and** as WASM, merge-blocking; manifest completeness failure fails the job rather than warning; blueprint/testing.md:202 lists the WASM KAT run in the PR gate.</result>

<result>## 1. Trustless Gateway — block, CAR, `dag-scope`, `entity-bytes`

Source: https://specs.ipfs.tech/http-gateways/trustless-gateway/ — **Trust: HIGH (normative IPFS spec)**

**Raw block responses** (`application/vnd.ipld.raw`):
> "An opaque bytes matching the requested block CID (`application/vnd.ipld.raw`). The Body hash MUST match the Multihash from the requested CID."

This is the load-bearing sentence for your question: the block response is **all-or-nothing**. Because the body must hash to the requested multihash, the raw-block path *cannot* serve a partial block — a sub-block range would fail verification. There is no sub-block retrieval unit in the trustless gateway.

**CAR responses** (`application/vnd.ipld.car`): "with optional `order` and `dups` params, path and optional `dag-scope` and `entity-bytes` URL parameters."

**`dag-scope=(block|entity|all)`**, default `all`, CAR only:
- `block` — "Only the root block at the end of the path is returned after blocks required to verify the specified path segments."
- `entity` — "For queries that traverse UnixFS data, `entity` roughly means return blocks needed to verify the terminating element of the requested content path. For UnixFS, all the blocks needed to read an entire UnixFS file, or enumerate a UnixFS directory. For all queries that reference non-UnixFS data, `entity` is equivalent to `block`."
- `all` — "Transmit the entire contiguous DAG that begins at the end of the path query, after blocks required to verify path segments."
- "When present, returned `Etag` must include unique prefix based on the passed scope type."

**`entity-bytes=from:to`** (CAR only; implies `dag-scope=entity`; "serves as a trustless equivalent of an HTTP Range Request"). The key normative sentence — **blocks are the unit, not bytes**:
> "can be interpreted as a continuous array of bytes (such as a UnixFS file), a Gateway MUST return only the minimal set of **blocks** necessary to verify the specified byte range of that entity."
> "When dealing with a sharded UnixFS file (`dag-pb`, `0x70`) and a non-zero `from` value, the UnixFS data and `blocksizes` determine the corresponding starting block for a given `from` offset."

So: **a byte range maps to the set of whole leaf blocks covering it, plus the intermediate blocks needed to verify them.** The gateway returns whole blocks — it never trims a leaf block to the requested byte boundary (it can't; the CAR consumer verifies each block against its CID). Byte-precise trimming is the *client's* job after verification.

Other `entity-bytes` rules (verbatim):
- "`from` value gives the byte-offset of the first byte in a range. `to` value gives the byte-offset of the last byte in the range; that is, the byte positions specified are inclusive."
- "`*` can be substituted for end-of-file — `entity-bytes=0:*` is the entire file (a verifiable version of HTTP request for `Range: 0-`)"
- "Negative numbers can be used for referring to bytes from the end of a file — `entity-bytes=-1024:*` is the last 1024 bytes of a file… It is also permissible (unlike with HTTP Range Requests) to ask for the range of 500 bytes from the beginning of the file to 1000 bytes from the end: `entity-bytes=499:-1000`"
- "If the terminating entity … cannot be interpreted as a continuous array of bytes (such as a DAG-CBOR/JSON map or UnixFS directory), the parameter MUST be ignored, and the request is equivalent to `dag-scope=entity`."
- "A Gateway MUST augment the returned `Etag` based on the passed `entity-bytes`."
- "A Gateway SHOULD return an HTTP 400 Bad Request error when the requested range is entirely outside of the entity's byte range and the Gateway is able to determine this upfront."
- Partial overlap: "the response MUST include the subset of blocks within the entity's bytes. This allows clients to request valid ranges of the entity without needing to know its total size beforehand…"
- Zero-length / fully-outside range: "the response is equivalent to `dag-scope=block`."

Streaming commitment (§3.1.2): "For CAR responses, once a gateway begins streaming (after successfully loading the root block), it has committed to HTTP `200 OK`." Note `entity-bytes` responses are **200, not 206** — it is a query parameter, not an HTTP `Range` header.

## 2. Path Gateway — HTTP `Range`

Source: https://specs.ipfs.tech/http-gateways/path-gateway/ — **Trust: HIGH**

- "`Range` can be used for requesting specific byte range of UnixFS files and raw blocks."
- "Gateways SHOULD support single range requests. The support of more than one range is optional: implementation MAY decide to not support more than one range."
- "Gateway implementations SHOULD be smart enough to require only the minimal DAG subset necessary for handling the range request."
- 206: "Partial Content: range request succeeded. Returned when requested range of data described by `Range` header of the request."
- "`Accept-Ranges: none` should be returned with `application/vnd.ipld.car` responses if the block order in CAR stream is not deterministic."

**Granularity answer:** the path gateway serves **byte-precise** ranges to the HTTP client (it is a trusted, deserialized response — the gateway reassembles and slices), but internally it must fetch **whole leaf blocks** covering the range ("minimal DAG subset"). The spec does not state a byte-alignment requirement on the response; it states a *fetch-efficiency* SHOULD on the backend. So: byte-exact on the wire, block-granular in retrieval cost.

## 3. CAR framing overhead

Source: https://ipld.io/specs/transport/car/carv1/ — **Trust: HIGH**

Layout, verbatim:
> `[ varint | DAG-CBOR block ] [ varint | CID | block ] [ varint | CID | block ] [ varint | CID | block ] …`

- Header: varint gives "the number of bytes beyond the varint itself that contain the *Header* block"; header is DAG-CBOR `{version: Int, roots: [&Any]}`.
- Each data section: varint = "the number of bytes containing the remainder of the section" — i.e. **len(CID bytes) + len(block payload), excluding the varint itself**. Then raw CID bytes (CIDv0 or CIDv1, self-describing/variable width), then the payload.

**Computed per-block overhead** (my arithmetic, not a spec quote): CIDv1 + raw (`0x55`) or dag-pb (`0x70`) + sha2-256 = `01 <codec> 12 20` + 32-byte digest = **36 bytes**. For a 256 KiB (262144 B) leaf, section length = 262180, which needs a **3-byte** unsigned varint (< 2^21). Total per-block framing = **39 bytes ≈ 0.0149 %** of a 256 KiB leaf. A one-root CARv1 header is ~59–60 bytes total (1-byte varint + DAG-CBOR map with one 36-byte CID). CARv2 adds an 11-byte pragma + 40-byte header + optional index — https://ipld.io/specs/transport/car/carv2/.

## 4. RFC 9110 §14 — may a server return more than requested?

Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt (fetched full text) — **Trust: HIGH (IETF standard)**

- **§14.2:** "A server **MAY** ignore the Range header field. However, origin servers and intermediate caches ought to support byte ranges when possible…" → returning the **whole representation with 200** is explicitly permitted.
- **§14.2:** "If all of the preconditions are true, the server supports the Range header field …, and that ranges-specifier is satisfiable …, the server **SHOULD** send a 206 (Partial Content) response with content containing one or more partial representations that correspond to the satisfiable range-spec(s) requested."
- **§14.2:** "The above does not imply that a server will send all requested ranges. In some cases, it may only be possible (or efficient) to send a portion of the requested ranges first, while expecting the client to re-request the remaining portions later…"
- **§15.3.7:** "A server that supports range requests will usually attempt to satisfy all of the requested ranges… However, a server might want to send only a subset of the data requested for reasons of its own, such as temporary unavailability, cache efficiency, load balancing, etc. Since a 206 response is self-descriptive, the client can still understand a response that only partially satisfies its range request."
- **§15.3.7:** "A client **MUST** inspect a 206 response's Content-Type and Content-Range field(s) to determine what parts are enclosed and whether additional requests are needed."
- **§15.3.7.1:** "If a single part is being transferred, the server generating the 206 response **MUST** generate a Content-Range header field, describing what range of the selected representation is enclosed, and a content consisting of the range."
- **§14.1.2:** "The first-pos value … gives the offset of the first byte in a range. The last-pos value gives the offset of the last byte in the range; that is, the byte positions specified are inclusive. Byte offsets start at zero." Absent `last-pos` (or ≥ length) ⇒ "remainder of the representation."
- **§14.4:** `Content-Range = range-unit SP ( range-resp / unsatisfied-range )`; "a sender SHOULD indicate the complete length of the representation from which the range has been extracted, unless the complete length is unknown."

**Direct answer:** RFC 9110 gives **explicit permission to send less** than requested (206 with a narrower Content-Range) and **explicit permission to send everything** (ignore Range, 200 OK). It gives **no explicit permission to send a 206 whose range is a strict superset** of what was asked — but it isn't forbidden either: §15.3.7.1 only requires that Content-Range accurately *describe* what is enclosed. **Caveat (my read, not a quote):** widening a 206 is risky in practice — clients that trust their own offsets (and §15.3.7 clients that "inspect Content-Range") will handle it, but many naive consumers won't. The clean, unambiguously spec-blessed way to return a whole block is **200 with the full block** (§14.2 "MAY ignore the Range header field"), which is exactly what the trustless gateway does with `entity-bytes`.

This is the weakest area for authoritative sources — flagging explicitly.

- **W3C MSE:** I found **no** normative guidance on HTTP range/chunk sizes. MSE (https://www.w3.org/TR/media-source-2/) defines `appendBuffer` on `ArrayBuffer` segments and is deliberately silent on how the app fetches them. **Could not find an authoritative number.**
- **HLS (RFC 8216, Trust: HIGH):** https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8216.html — §4.3.3.1 `EXT-X-TARGETDURATION`: "The EXTINF duration of each Media Segment in the Playlist file, when rounded to the nearest integer, MUST be less than or equal to the target duration." §4.3.2.2 `EXT-X-BYTERANGE`: "indicates that a Media Segment is a sub-range of the resource identified by its URI" — i.e. HLS byte-range addressing is *authored*, aligned to segment boundaries chosen by the packager, not arbitrary client-chosen ranges.
- **Apple HLS Authoring Specification** (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/http-live-streaming/hls-authoring-specification-for-apple-devices): the widely-cited requirement is a **6-second target duration**. **I could not fetch the page body verbatim** (JS-rendered); treat the "6 s" number as unverified-by-me though it is Apple's documented recommendation. **Trust: MEDIUM (couldn't confirm text).**
- **Fastly Segmented Caching** (https://www.fastly.com/documentation/guides/full-site-delivery/caching/segmented-caching/ and https://www.fastly.com/documentation/reference/vcl/variables/segmented-caching/segmented-caching-block-size/): the VCL variable `segmented_caching.block_size` is defined verbatim as "The number of bytes constituting each block-aligned file segment." 1. No spec permits or forbids a **206 with a superset range**; RFC 9110 only requires Content-Range to describe what's sent. Returning a whole block is cleanly spec-legal as **200** (§14.2 "MAY ignore the Range header field"), not as a widened 206.

`SealedChunk` is `{cid, sealed}` where `cid` is just `compute_cid(0x55, sealed)` (`chunk.rs:94`) — derivable, not independent data. And `root_block` is derivable from the leaves plus size and chunk size. So the only truly non-derivable thing is the sealed leaf bytes themselves; everything else is recomputable at drain, cheaply.

One landmine worth naming before you choose: **a multi-key scheme would break existing GC.** `orphan_staging_keys` (`staging.rs:88-111`) builds its `referenced` set from `op.staging_key()` — exactly one key per op — and classes *every* other staged key as an orphan. Per-block keys would be GC'd out from under the op that needs them.

questions.question: What does the single staged blob contain, given SealedContent is a root block plus N leaf blocks?

options.label: Root block + concatenated leaves
options.description: Blob = length-prefixed DAG root block, then the sealed leaves concatenated. Boundaries recover from the root manifest (chunkSize, size, links.len()), since every leaf but the last is chunkSize + 40 bytes (24 nonce + 16 tag). Leaf CIDs and content_cid re-derive at drain, and each parsed leaf can be CID-verified against its link before upload — a free fail-closed integrity check on the staged blob. Reuses the already-frozen root format instead of inventing one. Recommended.
options.preview:
[u32 root_len][root_block][leaf_0][leaf_1]...[leaf_n]

root manifest gives: chunkSize, size, links[]
  → leaf_i len = chunkSize + 40   (i < n)
  → leaf_n len = size - chunkSize*n + 40
  → verify compute_cid(leaf_i) == links[i]  (fail-closed)

options.label: Concatenated leaves only
options.description: Smallest blob. Boundaries parsed using the ContentProfile in effect at drain time, root block and all CIDs re-derived. Fragile: a queued op that survives an app upgrade whose chunk size changed becomes unparseable, and there is no self-describing check that the blob is intact.

options.label: Serialized SealedContent
options.description: A new internal encoding (det-CBOR or serde) carrying root block, content_cid, and every leaf with its CID explicitly. Fully self-describing, no derivation at drain. Costs a new internal wire format that must itself be versioned, and stores data that is already derivable — which also inflates the staging budget accounting.

options.label: One staging key per block
options.description: Op's key becomes a manifest key; blocks live under derived keys. Requires reworking orphan_staging_keys and its exact-match referenced set, or the per-block blobs get GC'd as orphans. Rejected unless there is a reason to want per-block addressing at drain.
